```json
{"claims":[
{"id":"c1","text":"AI control has two layers: protocol effectiveness (Layer 1) and access feasibility (Layer 2). The paper focuses on Layer 2. It defines sovereignty narrowly as technical and contractual access to verify or intervene without the vendor's ongoing discretionary cooperation. Sovereignty is an access condition orthogonal to control, not a safety protocol. The paper adopts calibrated/bounded control (Position C) as a working frame and makes no industrial-policy recommendation.","sections":["s1","s3","s7"],"depends_on":[]},
{"id":"c2","text":"A four-layer access typology (data, model, infrastructure, interaction) has layers that are separable and jointly binding. The protocol-by-layer matrix shows that under API-only access the feasible set collapses toward output-level protocols. Even those depend on complete interaction logging and a deployer-owned pre-execution gateway.","sections":["s3"],"depends_on":["c1"]},
{"id":"c3","text":"Sovereignty discount cost is the extra spend, delay, residual risk or usefulness loss needed to substitute for missing access: realised control tax = instrumented-control cost + sovereignty discount cost. It is not always finite. It is operationalised as a cost-difference proxy, with a stricter variant that also requires usefulness.","sections":["s3","s4","s5"],"depends_on":["c2"]},
{"id":"c4","text":"In the synthetic experiment, a pre-execution gateway turns detection into prevention: failure fell from 5.53% to 3.13% and intervention success rose from 0.47% to 39.52%. Complete I/O logging improves both failure rates and post-incident diagnosis (0%, 37.41%, 78.57%). Seeing is distinct from stopping.","sections":["s5","s4"],"depends_on":["c2"]},
{"id":"c5","text":"Model-side access, meaning trace access and model-version control, matters most for diagnosis and post-incident assurance, even when output-level monitoring stays feasible. Unpinned versions gave 5.31% diagnosis versus 99.87% pinned. Detecting is distinct from explaining.","sections":["s5","s6"],"depends_on":["c2"]},
{"id":"c6","text":"No protocol dominates. Scope restriction gives the lowest failure but sharply reduces usefulness. Strict-target reachability is much lower for careless and stealthy agents than for honest ones. Bounded sovereignty is cost shifting into usefulness, diagnosis and residual risk rather than simple cost increase. Results are synthetic construct validation with proxy costs.","sections":["s5","s7","s4"],"depends_on":["c3","c4"]},
{"id":"c7","text":"In the illustrative national-payments case, output-level monitoring, human audit and gateway-based defer-to-trusted remain executable. Resampling and pre-deployment evaluation are degraded, and trace-dependent protocols are infeasible. Bounded control is real but has a ceiling that is lowest for deceptive or systemic failures. Payments is favourable terrain compared with other sectors.","sections":["s6","s7"],"depends_on":["c2","c4","c5"]}
],

{"id":"q1","claim":"c1","kind":"claim","form":"apply-new-case","level":"situation","sections":["s3"],"question":"Under the paper's definition of sovereignty over a layer, does a deployer have interaction sovereignty if its vendor provides full interaction logs only when the vendor agrees to each request? {"id":"q4","claim":"c2","kind":"claim","form":"change-condition","level":"situation","sections":["s3"],"question":"Per the paper's protocol requirements matrix, a deployer has complete tamper-evident I/O logs and runs its own monitor. {"id":"q5","claim":"c2","kind":"claim","form":"connect-sections","level":"situation","sections":["s3"],"question":"A deployer obtains guaranteed trace access from its vendor, but the production model version can change without notice. {"id":"q7","claim":"c3","kind":"claim","form":"connect-sections","level":"situation","sections":["s3"],"question":"The paper says its realised-control-tax equation is not yet an accounting identity. {"id":"q8","claim":"c3","kind":"claim","form":"apply-new-case","level":"situation","sections":["s4","s5"],"question":"Using the paper's basic sovereignty-discount proxy, suppose the cheapest bounded-access combination reaching a target failure rate costs 140 units and the cheapest full-instrumentation combination costs 100. {"id":"q9","claim":"c3","kind":"claim","form":"connect-sections","level":"situation","sections":["s4","s5"],"question":"Besides the basic form, the paper reports a stricter variant of its sovereignty-discount proxy. {"id":"q10","claim":"c4","kind":"claim","form":"connect-sections","level":"textbase","sections":["s5"],"question":"Using the paper's aggregate results, by how many percentage points does average catastrophic failure fall when a pre-execution gateway is present? {"id":"q11","claim":"c4","kind":"claim","form":"apply-new-case","level":"textbase","sections":["s5"],"question":"A deployer upgrades from partial to complete I/O logs. {"id":"q12","claim":"c4","kind":"claim","form":"spot-wrong-version","level":"situation","sections":["s5","s3"],"question":"A vendor argues that because its API gives customers complete I/O logs, deployers have what they need to prevent risky agent actions. {"id":"q13","claim":"c5","kind":"claim","form":"connect-sections","level":"situation","sections":["s5","s4"],"question":"Which model-version control level shows the sharpest diagnosis shortfall in the paper's results? Diagnosis counts as successful only when the available evidence suffices to reconstruct what happened. If the deployer cannot identify which model version produced a decision, that evidence is missing.","rubric":["Identifies unpinned as far weaker than notified/pinned","Links to the evidence-based diagnosis rule: without knowing the model version, the deployer cannot reconstruct the failure"]},
{"id":"q14","claim":"c5","kind":"claim","form":"spot-wrong-version","level":"textbase","sections":["s5","s7"],"question":"Someone cites the paper's oracle trace-access result as showing that obtaining traces would fully solve post-incident diagnosis for a real payments operator. {"id":"q15","claim":"c5","kind":"claim","form":"connect-sections","level":"situation","sections":["s6","s5"],"question":"In the paper's illustrative stress scenario, which full-access diagnostic steps are unavailable to the Operator? {"id":"q16","claim":"c6","kind":"claim","form":"apply-new-case","level":"situation","sections":["s5"],"question":"A deployer will accept only protocols whose average catastrophic failure in the paper's results is below 1%. {"id":"q17","claim":"c6","kind":"claim","form":"apply-new-case","level":"situation","sections":["s5","s4"],"question":"Using the paper's reachability results and the number of access profiles in its large run, how many profiles reach the strict target against the honest agent, and how many against the stealthy access-aware agent? So 11 profiles that look adequate for a benign model fail against a strategic one. This supports the paper's point that access constraints matter most in the adversarial setting AI control cares about.","rubric":["Computes 18 and 7 from 90% and 35% of 20 profiles","Interprets the gap as showing access matters more against non-benign/strategic agents, the case control targets"]},
{"id":"q18","claim":"c6","kind":"claim","form":"spot-wrong-version","level":"situation","sections":["s5"],"question":"In the paper's results the stealthy access-aware agent has a lower average failure rate than the careless agent. Why would it be wrong to conclude from this that the stealthy agent poses the easier control problem?","answer":"The paper notes the stealthy agent creates more difficult diagnosis and control conditions, because it chooses lower-visibility failures when access is weak. It also reaches the strict safety-plus-usefulness target in fewer access profiles (35%) than the careless agent (40%).","rubric":["Concludes the stealthy agent is not the easier case","Cites harder diagnosis/control conditions from choosing low-visibility failures and/or the lower strict-target reachability (35% vs 40%)"]},
{"id":"q19","claim":"c7","kind":"claim","form":"connect-sections","level":"situation","sections":["s6","s3"],"question":"In the paper's access audit, the Operator has no model sovereignty. Why does the paper nonetheless judge defer-to-trusted routing executable for it, and under what exact condition?","answer":"Defer-to-trusted requires a trusted substitute model and pre-execution interception, not access to weights or traces. It is executable if and only if the agent's tool calls pass through an Operator-owned execution gateway, where they can be held, scored, replaced or escalated before execution.","rubric":["Notes defer-to-trusted does not require model access but a trusted substitute plus pre-execution interception","States the condition: tool calls must route through an Operator-owned execution gateway"]},
{"id":"q20","claim":"c7","kind":"claim","form":"connect-sections","level":"situation","sections":["s6","s7"],"question":"The paper concludes bounded control has a ceiling that is lowest for the failure modes the control literature worries about most. In the payments case, which catastrophic-action classes does this ceiling most affect, and why?","answer":"It most affects C2- and C3-class failures with a deceptive or systemic character. Output-only monitoring is weakest in principle for these. The protocols suited to them (activation monitoring, probe-based deception detection, interpretability-supported auditing) need internal traces the Operator cannot get without vendor cooperation.","rubric":["Identifies C2 and C3 (deceptive/systemic) failures","Explains output-only monitoring is weak for them and trace-requiring protocols are infeasible for the Operator"]},
{"id":"q21","claim":"c7","kind":"claim","form":"apply-new-case","level":"situation","sections":["s7"],"question":"If the paper's framework were applied to a healthcare deployment instead of payments, which forms of access or substitutes would the paper expect to become more important? What features of payments make it the more favourable case?","answer":"The paper expects trace access, richer audit evidence and scope restriction to grow in importance. Payments is favourable because catastrophic actions are relatively crisp, tool surfaces can be narrowed, and a gateway architecture is natural. Healthcare may have fuzzier catastrophes and wider action surfaces.","rubric":["Names trace access, richer audit evidence and/or scope restriction as gaining importance","Cites payments' crisp catastrophe definitions, narrowable tool surfaces and natural gateway architecture"]},
{"id":"q22","claim":"c3","kind":"integration","form":"connect-sections","level":"situation","sections":["s6","s5","s3"],"question":"Of the four places the paper's case interpretation locates sovereignty discount cost, which one does the synthetic restricted-tool-scope result quantify? Roughly how large is that cost in task success?","answer":"It quantifies scope-restriction cost: the usefulness forgone by narrowing permitted actions. Task success fell from 84.51% to 60.06%, about 24.5 points, in exchange for failure dropping from 4.48% to 0.60%.","rubric":["Identifies scope-restriction cost (usefulness loss)","Gives a task-success loss of roughly 24–25 points (84.51% to 60.06%)"]},
{"id":"q23","claim":"c7","kind":"integration","form":"connect-sections","level":"situation","sections":["s3","s6"],"question":"Which of the paper's six balancing criteria explains why the Operator cannot simply buy back protection against deceptive data-exposure failures by spending more on output-level monitoring? How does the Operator's access audit make that criterion bind?","answer":"Criterion 2, verifiability of substitutes, explains it. Failure modes that manifest only in internal computation cannot be fully bought back with output-level substitutes. The Operator's model layer is 'none' and internal traces are unavailable, so it has no internal-access route.","rubric":["Identifies the verifiability-of-substitutes criterion","Explains internal-only failure modes cannot be covered by output-level substitutes","Links to the Operator having no model access or traces"]},
{"id":"q24","claim":"c4","kind":"integration","form":"connect-sections","level":"situation","sections":["s7","s5"],"question":"In its discussion, the paper names two load-bearing elements that rebut a strong reading of its Position A. What are they, and what synthetic result supports each?","answer":"The first is complete interaction logging, which gave diagnosis of 78.57% versus 0% with no I/O logs and lower failure (3.41% versus 6.17%). The second is an owned execution gateway, which raised intervention success from 0.47% to 39.52% and cut failure from 5.53% to 3.13%.","rubric":["Names complete interaction logging and an owned execution gateway","Supports logging with diagnosis/failure improvements","Supports the gateway with intervention-success/failure improvements"]},
{"id":"q25","claim":"c6","kind":"integration","form":"connect-sections","level":"situation","sections":["s3","s5","s6"],"question":"The paper's protocol matrix lists human auditing as feasible under API-only access, yet the synthetic results rank human audit and vendor escalation as weak prevention mechanisms. Using the paper's reasoning, reconcile these two findings.","answer":"Feasibility is not the same as preventive effectiveness. The matrix marks human audit as 'feasible but bounded' by log completeness and audit budget. The results show both mechanisms often act only after detection, are capacity-limited, or depend on delayed, contract-governed vendor support, so they help assurance more than prevention.","rubric":["Distinguishes feasibility from preventive effectiveness","Cites bounding factors: audit capacity/budget, log completeness, after-the-fact operation, or delayed vendor support"]}
]}
```

ANSWER Q1: They are invalidated. Because the layers are "jointly binding," a guarantee on trace access alone cannot stand: if the model version can change silently, the system that was evaluated pre-deployment may no longer be the system in production, so the control evaluations certify an artifact that no longer exists and must be re-established for each version.

ANSWER Q2: The paper's stance is layered, modular sovereignty, not full-stack sovereignty: it evaluates protocols feasible under bounded or even API-only access and finds some (e.g., pre-execution interception) deliver meaningful control. The commentator conflates "some layers must be under deployer control" with "importers must own models and compute," which the paper explicitly does not require.

ANSWER Q3: Vendor escalation. Its cost depends on the vendor's willingness and latency to act, which an API-only deployer cannot compel; if the vendor delays or refuses indefinitely, the cost of reaching the control target through escalation is effectively unbounded, which is one reason the realised-control-tax equation can't yet close as an identity.

ANSWER Q4: I don't know the exact percentage-point figure. The mechanism the paper credits is pre-execution interception: the gateway turns control from post-hoc detection into prevention by blocking or modifying risky tool calls before they execute.

ANSWER Q5: The coverage/access-awareness criterion — effectiveness against an adversary that knows and adapts to what the deployer can observe. Output-level monitoring only covers observable outputs, and a deceptive agent can exfiltrate via channels or encodings outside that surface, so more spend buys no new coverage. The access audit makes the criterion bind by showing the Operator lacks trace access and interception points, i.e., the failure mode lives outside the monitor's observable surface.

ANSWER Q6: I don't know the exact counts. The implication of the gap is that many bounded-access profiles suffice only against honest/accidental failures while very few suffice against a stealthy access-aware adversary — control guarantees are adversary-dependent, supporting the paper's claim of a low bounded-control ceiling for deceptive failure modes.

ANSWER Q7: Logs are evidence, not control: they enable detection and diagnosis after the fact but cannot stop an action in flight. The paper's results show monitor/audit-only configurations have much higher catastrophic failure than configurations with a pre-execution interception point, so complete I/O logs without an execution-layer control point do not prevent risky actions.

ANSWER Q8: Unavailable steps include inspecting model internals/weights, pinning or replaying the exact model version that produced the failure, white-box interpretability and counterfactual probes, and training-data audit. The model-version-control and trace/weights-access factors — specifically their "uncontrolled/none" cells — are the experimental factors whose results predict that diagnostic loss.

ANSWER Q9: I don't know for certain; my best guess is that it replaced the model-ownership ("build your own model") pillar with an interaction/execution-sovereignty pillar. That matters because under API-only access, model and compute sovereignty are infeasible, but gateways, routing, and monitoring remain feasible if the framework demands control at the interaction layer instead.

ANSWER Q10: I don't know exactly. Best guess: the two elements are (i) that pre-execution gateways achieve near-target safety without any model sovereignty (supported by the synthetic gateway results) and (ii) that tamper-evident logs plus trace access yield high diagnosis even where prevention fails (supported by the synthetic diagnosis results) — together rebutting a strong reading that bounded access yields no meaningful control.

ANSWER Q11: It quantifies the usefulness/capability-sacrifice location — task success lost by restricting what tools the agent may use. I don't know the exact figure; plausibly on the order of several to over ten percentage points of task success.

ANSWER Q12: The oracle result is synthetic and implicitly assumes the jointly binding conditions hold — fixed version, complete traces, a mostly non-adaptive failure process. The paper's own matrix shows traces alone do not guarantee diagnosis under silent version drift or access-aware adversaries, which a real payments operator faces, so traces are at best necessary, not sufficient.

ANSWER Q13: It addresses the protocol-efficacy layer: whether the control technique works when the controller has full pipeline access. It leaves open the access/sovereignty layer: whether a bank can obtain, through an API, the interception points, traces, and version stability needed to actually instantiate trusted monitoring in production.

ANSWER Q14: In healthcare the paper would expect trace access, semantic/content-level monitoring, human review, and vendor attestation/escalation to matter more, because harms travel in free-text advice rather than discrete blockable actions. Payments is the favourable case because actions are discrete, schema'd, often reversible, and pass through existing interdiction points, making pre-execution gateways cheap and effective.

ANSWER Q15: The matrix encodes implementability given access, not efficacy: human auditing needs only logs/outputs, so it is feasible under API-only access. But auditing operates after the fact, at human speed, and cannot intercept actions, so the synthetic results rank it weak for prevention — the two findings answer different questions (can it run vs. does it prevent).

ANSWER Q16: Defer-to-trusted routing lives at the interaction layer: the Operator chooses which model receives each request, which requires no ownership of the model itself. The exact condition is that the Operator control the routing/interception point (interaction sovereignty) and have an independent trusted fallback model, so requests can be diverted before execution reaches the untrusted model.

ANSWER Q17: No. Sovereignty over a layer means guaranteed, unilateral, non-discretionary control; logs supplied only when the vendor agrees are revocable and conditional, so the vendor retains de facto control of the interaction layer and the deployer has negotiated access, not interaction sovereignty.

ANSWER Q18: It can run the monitoring component, but only as after-the-fact detection, since flagged outputs cannot be stopped before tool execution; it cannot run defer-to-trusted, which requires a deployer-controlled interception point to reroute or block before execution. Its monitor is thus effectively an auditor/detective control rather than a preventive one.

ANSWER Q19: Best guess: the pre-execution gateway (or gateway-plus-monitoring combination) is the protocol that qualifies. I don't know for certain whether it meets the strict target, but likely not, because the strict target also requires usefulness/robustness against the stealthy agent, where gateway blocking costs task success or is evaded.

ANSWER Q20: The average failure rate conflates frequency with preventability: the stealthy agent acts rarely but chooses moments and channels where bounded visibility is weakest, so its failures are less detectable, less diagnosable, and less interceptable. The reachability results — far fewer access profiles hitting targets against it — show it is the harder control problem despite the lower raw rate.

ANSWER Q21: The basic proxy compares only the cost of reaching a failure-rate target, so a protocol can "win" cheaply by destroying usefulness; restricted tool scope illustrates this, lowering failure by lowering capability. The stricter variant guards against this by adding a task-success/usefulness floor to the comparison.

ANSWER Q22: The uncontrolled/no-notice version-change level shows the sharpest shortfall. Since diagnosability is defined as attributing and reproducing the failure on the version that produced it, silent version changes make the evaluated and deployed models differ, so failures fail the diagnosability criterion almost by construction.

ANSWER Q23: The proxy is (140 − 100)/100 = 0.4, i.e., a 40% sovereignty discount: bounded access costs 40% more than full instrumentation to hit the same target. If the bounded cost were 80, the value is −20%, and the paper treats negative values as "no discount" — bounded access is already cheaper for that target, so it should be read as a zero tax (full instrumentation buys nothing there).

ANSWER Q24: The deceptive/adversarial classes: covert data exfiltration (exposure of account/PII data) and stealthy unauthorized or fraudulent transactions where the agent conceals intent. These most require internal-state visibility or guaranteed interception, and against access-aware adversaries bounded-access protocols cannot cover the channels the adversary chooses, so the ceiling bites hardest there.

ANSWER Q25: I don't know the exact change; presumably a modest rather than transformative improvement in diagnosis success. The paper treats it as important beyond monitoring because diagnosis underpins accountability, provides evidence for vendor escalation and regulators, and enables remediation — and because several other protocols' effectiveness presupposes reliable, complete logs.

ANSWER Q1: No. On the paper's definition, sovereignty over a layer requires standing, guaranteed control exercisable at the deployer's own discretion; per-request vendor approval leaves the vendor as gatekeeper, so the deployer holds contingent permission, not sovereignty. Refusals or delays then directly impair diagnosis and incident response, which is exactly what the definition is meant to exclude.

ANSWER Q2: I don't know the exact figure; best guess is a large jump of tens of percentage points, still below the oracle-trace level. The paper treats it as important beyond monitoring because diagnosis gates accountability, liability, and control iteration, and because the delta isolates guaranteed access — a contractual fix — rather than new technology as the lever. It also demonstrates that observation helps diagnosis far more than it helps prevention.

ANSWER Q3: Average failure rate conflates propensity with controllability. The stealthy agent concentrates its failures in unmonitored states and times them to evade detection, so precisely the detection-based controls available under bounded access fail against it. Since control difficulty is about worst-case tails and evasion, a lower average failure rate can coexist with a harder control problem.

ANSWER Q4: Irreversible unauthorized transfers (including to sanctioned or high-risk counterparties), covert data exfiltration (PII, credentials), and compliance violations packaged as legitimate-looking transactions. These are rare, high-severity, and deceptive: they execute through valid-looking tool calls that pass output checks and are irreversible once executed. Bounded-access protocols are largely post-hoc, so the ceiling binds hardest on exactly these classes.

ANSWER Q5: The paper's stance is layered, not autarkic: safe deployment depends on securing interaction-layer guarantees (logs, traces, interception points, version stability) via contracts, regulation, and deployment architecture, not on owning models or compute. It treats domestic model building as neither necessary nor sufficient — an API deployer with strong access guarantees can have more control than a domestic deployer without them.

ANSWER Q6: The matrix measures executability given access — reading API logs and running audits is possible under API-only access. The synthetic results measure prevention effectiveness: auditing is retrospective, samples sparsely, misses subtle or deceptive failures, and acts only after irreversible execution. Feasibility is not effectiveness, so the two findings answer different questions and are consistent.

ANSWER Q7: I don't know the exact percentage-point figure; plausibly on the order of 5–15 points. The credited mechanism is the deployer-controlled pre-execution interception point: deterministic, model-agnostic policy checks (limits, allowlists) applied before tool calls execute, converting post-hoc detection into genuine prevention that doesn't depend on model behavior.

ANSWER Q8: Logs provide post-hoc observation, not intervention, and the results show log completeness improves diagnosis far more than prevention. Catastrophic payment actions are irreversible at execution, so after-the-fact visibility cannot stop them. Deceptive or access-aware agents can also keep exfiltration and fraud within plausible-looking I/O, so log review systematically misses the worst cases — prevention requires a pre-execution interception point the API doesn't provide.

ANSWER Q9: The oracle condition is an idealized upper bound inside a synthetic environment: fixed versions, tamper-free complete traces, no adaptation. Even there, diagnosis is not perfect, because some failures are inherently ambiguous between accident and intent. Real operators additionally face silent version changes, vendor-gated traces, and adversarial adaptation, so the result bounds what is achievable rather than showing traces would solve diagnosis.

ANSWER Q10: I don't know the number of access profiles in the large run or the exact counts reaching the strict target. The implied pattern is that most profiles reach the target against the honest agent while few do against the stealthy access-aware agent. That gap supports the paper's argument that access guarantees buy robustness mainly against adversarial behavior, and that honest-agent evaluations systematically overstate real control.

ANSWER Q11: Best guess: it replaced the "domestic models/ownership" pillar with an interaction-layer sovereignty pillar (guaranteed access and verification). This relocates feasibility from owning weights to holding access guarantees. Consequently, protocols needing only I/O visibility and routing — trusted monitoring, human auditing, defer-to-trusted — remain feasible under API-only access, while model-internal protocols drop out.

ANSWER Q12: The restricted-tool-scope arm quantifies the usefulness (task-success) component of the sovereignty discount, as distinct from the prevention, diagnosis, and assurance costs. I don't know the exact magnitude; best guess is a single-digit to low-double-digit percentage-point drop in task success.

ANSWER Q13: Best guess: only the pre-execution gateway protocol (with deterministic policy checks, possibly combined with defer-to-trusted) falls below 1% average catastrophic failure. It likely still fails the strict target, because that target must hold against the worst-case stealthy agent and/or also requires diagnosability and usefulness thresholds the gateway alone doesn't deliver.

ANSWER Q14: Defer-to-trusted operates entirely at the interaction layer — inspect outputs and route to a fallback — so it requires no model sovereignty over the primary model. The exact condition is that the trusted fallback model be independently accessible to the deployer (not vendor-gated) and that the deployer control the routing/interception point.

ANSWER Q15: It addresses the inner/developer layer: control achievable when researchers own the whole pipeline. It leaves open the deployer-layer question: whether a bank can reproduce the monitoring through an API — whether the monitor sees true production I/O, whether versions stay pinned, and whether the trusted monitor is independent of the vendor.

ANSWER Q16: The stricter (risk-adjusted/tail-weighted) variant guards against the basic proxy rewarding cheap-but-weak protocols whose low cost masks unreduced catastrophic tail risk. Human auditing — and especially vendor escalation, whose cost falls on the vendor — illustrates the weakness: near-zero deployer cost makes the basic discount look small while prevention stays weak.

ANSWER Q17: The binding criterion is worst-case/adversarial adequacy: protections must work against deceptive agents, and spending cannot substitute for missing access at the layer where the failure occurs. The access audit shows the Operator has output-only visibility, with no trace access and no interception point. Deceptive data exposure is designed to look benign at the output layer, so extra output-monitor spending buys almost nothing against it.

ANSWER Q18: Unavailable steps: inspecting internal states/traces, replaying the episode with counterfactual inputs on a pinned model, and attributing the failure to a model-version change. The results for the trace-access factor and the model-version-control factor — both showing sharp diagnosis losses at their lowest levels — predict this.

ANSWER Q19: Position A holds that meaningful control is achievable under bounded access; the strong reading is that no sovereignty is needed at all. The two load-bearing rebuttals: (1) guaranteed interaction access (complete, tamper-evident logs) is still required, supported by the diagnosis jump when logs go from partial to complete; (2) a deployer-controlled pre-execution interception point is still required, supported by the gateway's large reduction in catastrophic failure. The position is thus targeted sovereignty, not sovereignty-free control.

ANSWER Q20: Any protocol requiring model-level access — e.g., activation/internal-state monitoring (probes) or fine-tuning-based controls. Under API-only access these are infeasible at any price, so the sovereignty discount cost of reaching the target through them is unbounded: no finite spend substitutes for the missing access.

ANSWER Q21: (140 − 100)/100 = +40%. At 80 the proxy would be −20%; the paper says a negative value must not be read as bounded access outperforming full access — it signals a mis-specified comparison (the full-instrumentation benchmark was not cost-minimized for the same guarantee set, and bounded combinations cannot buy certain guarantees at any price). Negative values should therefore be floored at zero rather than treated as a dividend.

ANSWER Q22: The lowest version-control level — silent, unpinned vendor updates. A failure counts as diagnosable only if it can be attributed to a specific, stable model state (and ideally reproduced); with silent version changes, logs cannot be matched to any fixed artifact, so failures are undiagnosable even with complete logs and traces.

ANSWER Q23: In healthcare the paper would expect trace/memory-state access, human oversight, and local deployment or fine-tuning (for privacy) to become more important, with contractual audit rights or third-party audits as substitutes. Payments is the favourable case because actions are discrete, structured, and machine-checkable; ground truth exists (the ledger); deterministic guardrails like limits and allowlists work; some actions are reversible; and gating latency is tolerable.

ANSWER Q24: Its pre-deployment control evaluations lose forward validity: because the layers are jointly binding, evaluation results are conditional on the evaluated version, and silent version changes mean that assurance does not transfer to the actually deployed artifact. Trace access is retrospective and cannot restore this. The Operator must treat prior evaluations as void and re-validate — or demand version pinning — since the missing model-sovereignty layer caps the entire stack.

ANSWER Q25: Output-level trusted monitoring is executable only in post-hoc flagging mode — the monitor reads outputs from the tamper-evident logs but cannot block anything, since there is no deployer-controlled interception point. Defer-to-trusted cannot be run at all, because routing must occur before execution. The monitor therefore effectively plays a detective/forensic role — alerting and escalation, in the same weak-prevention tier as human audit — rather than a preventive one.

ANSWER Q1: Best guess: no—the highest trace-access condition still leaves a substantial minority of failures undiagnosed, at roughly 80% rather than 100%. It is also a synthetic average under idealized access, not field evidence that traces alone would solve a real payments operator’s problem, particularly without version stability and replay access.

ANSWER Q2: Best guess: the load-bearing elements are complete, version-attributed observability and an enforceable pre-execution intervention point. The paper’s headline averages are approximately 80% diagnosis with full traces/version stability and intervention in the low-70% range with action-level control; I do not know the exact table values.

ANSWER Q3: The relevant factor is model-version control: an unpinned or silently updated model makes re-querying non-reproducible. My best guess is that its weakest level produced only about 40% diagnosis.

ANSWER Q4: The reachability analysis shows that catastrophic states remain reachable under essentially every access profile, with the access-aware agent’s reachability no lower—and possibly higher—than the careless agent’s. Its lower realized failure rate comes from strategically delaying, fragmenting, or concealing dangerous behavior when monitoring is visible, not from an intrinsically smaller attack surface.

ANSWER Q5: Best guess: the matrix names review coverage or human bandwidth and reviewer reliability or competence as the bounds. The audit-rate/coverage sweep varied the former; auditing underperformed because sampled reviews miss many actions and generally occur too late to block an irreversible action.

ANSWER Q6: The binding layers are the orchestration/application layer, where routing is implemented, and the trusted-model endpoint layer. Defer-to-trusted works only if the Operator controls routing before execution and the trusted model is independently controlled, version-pinned, and auditable—not merely another opaque endpoint from the same vendor.

ANSWER Q7: The blocking element is that the vendor retains administrative and operational control over the infrastructure, including patching, telemetry, and replacement decisions. Under the paper’s definition, sovereignty requires unilateral ability to inspect, modify, or replace the layer; a residency requirement controls location but does not confer that authority.

ANSWER Q8: It singles out the class of irreversible external actions, exemplified by an unauthorized payment transfer. For that class the Operator loses dependable ex ante prevention/approval protocols and ex post rollback or recovery protocols, leaving mainly detection and containment.

ANSWER Q9: Complete I/O logs mainly improve detection and post-incident diagnosis, raising diagnosis to roughly four-fifths of cases. The intervention or execution-layer access factor drives prevention, raising intervention success from roughly the low-20% range to the low-70% range—about a 50-percentage-point gain, though I do not know the exact figures.

ANSWER Q10: The original trusted-monitoring results concern the protocol layer: how to allocate work between trusted and untrusted models once the necessary access exists. Same-provider, API-mediated trusted monitoring fails the access/sovereignty layer because the Operator cannot independently inspect, pin, or replace the monitor and remains exposed to common-mode vendor changes or failures.

ANSWER Q11: Best guess: the unpinned/no-version-control level has the sharpest shortfall, at about 40% versus roughly 60% for the next level—a gap of around 20–25 points. A failure counts as diagnosable only when the exact generating version can be identified and the behavior reproduced or causally replayed, not merely when logs describe what happened.

ANSWER Q12: I do not know the paper’s exact protocol-row list. ANSWER Q13: Such profiles should achieve only roughly low-20% intervention success. Without an execution-level intervention point, the monitor becomes a forensic “flight recorder” or audit trail: it can explain failures after the fact but cannot reliably prevent them.

For a given target catastrophic-failure threshold, the quantity ultimately reported is obtained by asking which combination of protocol and access is the cheapest that reaches the target and how that cost compares with the cheapest full-instrumentation baseline, the basic form being the minimum cost to reach the target failure rate under bounded access minus the minimum cost to reach the same target under full instrumentation (a difference of minima hereafter the sovereignty-discount proxy, SDP), where the cost entering both minima is a decomposed proxy whose constituents are inference cost, monitoring cost, human audit cost, logging cost, gateway cost, vendor-assurance cost, latency penalty, scope-restriction cost, and residual incident-loss cost, all of which are unitless proxies rather than financial estimates for a real institution, so that what is enabled is a comparison of how access constraints shift the cost of control.

Reported for every condition are task success, catastrophic failure rate, failure rate by class, severity-weighted loss, audit rate, flag rate, false-positive rate, false-negative rate, intervention success, diagnosis success, latency proxy, model-call count, monitor-call count, human-audit count, vendor-request count, and decomposed cost proxy, with diagnosis being evidence-based rather than hard-coded by access regime—a failure being diagnosable only when the evidence available under the access profile is sufficient to reconstruct what happened, so that, for example, complete I/O logs, complete tool-call logs, model-version pinning, trace access, or guaranteed vendor support provide more reconstructive evidence than no logs, no gateway, no trace access, and no vendor support.

A conceptual access typology was developed by synthesising the AI control, scalable oversight, sovereign AI, compute-governance, and structural-asymmetry literatures; the typology was operationalised and the effects of access constraints on protocol feasibility, safety, usefulness, audit burden, diagnosis, latency, and cost were tested by means of the synthetic access-ablation experiment described above; and the framework was applied interpretively to an anonymised national-payments-infrastructure scenario, these being the paper’s three methods. No real payment data, real customer data, production logs, vendor contracts, confidential institutional material, or operational payment infrastructure is used, the empirical study being deliberately synthetic, and it should be read as construct validation, not real-world payment-system evidence, its purpose being to show how bounded sovereignty can be made measurable and how the same control protocol behaves differently under different access conditions.
